items.q: Match the following criteria to the source's diagnostic pillars — 1) Fasting plasma glucose 2) 2-hour post-load 3) HbA1c … A) ≥126 mg/dL B) ≥200 mg/dL C) ≥6.5%
items.exp: The three pillars are fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL, 2-hour post-load ≥200 mg/dL and HbA1c ≥6.5%; any one confirms diabetes in the absence of symptoms. (Book p917)

items.q: An asymptomatic 50-year-old has fasting plasma glucose 132 mg/dL on two occasions. Which diagnostic label is most appropriate?
items.exp: FPG ≥126 mg/dL confirmed on repeat testing confirms diabetes in an asymptomatic adult. (Book p917)

items.q: Assess these diagnostic facts: I HbA1c ≥6.5% is diagnostic. II A single abnormal test is sufficient if symptomatic.
items.exp: HbA1c ≥6.5% is one pillar of diagnosis; in symptomatic patients, a single random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with classic symptoms is diagnostic. (Book p917)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — a value NOT diagnostic of diabetes?
items.exp: HbA1c 5.9% is below the 6.5% threshold; HbA1c 7.0%, FPG 130 mg/dL and 2-h PG 220 mg/dL all meet diabetes criteria. (Book p917)

items.q: The three pillars of diabetes diagnosis on this page are fasting glucose, 2-hour post-load and ___.
items.exp: HbA1c is the third pillar; C-peptide, fructosamine and 1,5-AG are alternative markers but not part of the three-pillar definition. (Book p917)

items.q: Match the following glucose state to its FPG / 2-h PG range — 1) Normal 2) Pre-diabetes / IGT 3) Diabetes … A) FPG <100, 2-h PG <140 B) FPG 100–125 or 2-h PG 140–199 C) FPG ≥126 or 2-h PG ≥200
items.exp: Normal FPG is <100 mg/dL and 2-h PG <140 mg/dL; pre-diabetes (IFG / IGT) is FPG 100–125 or 2-h PG 140–199; diabetes is ≥126 or ≥200. (Book p917)

items.q: A 45-year-old has FPG 118 mg/dL, 2-h PG 175 mg/dL and HbA1c 6.1%. The most consistent diagnostic label is:
items.exp: Combined IFG (FPG 100–125) and IGT (2-h PG 140–199) with HbA1c 6.1% fits pre-diabetes. (Book p917)

items.q: Assess diagnostic reproducibility: I A diagnosis requires confirmation on repeat testing in asymptomatic patients. II HbA1c can be falsely low in haemoglobinopathies.
items.exp: Asymptomatic diagnosis is confirmed on repeat testing; HbA1c can be unreliable with haemoglobin variants, iron deficiency and pregnancy. (Book p917)

items.q: Match the following state to its characteristic finding — 1) Normal 2) Pre-diabetes 3) Diabetes 4) Stress hyperglycaemia … A) HbA1c <5.7% B) HbA1c 5.7–6.4% C) HbA1c ≥6.5% D) Transient rise during acute illness
items.exp: HbA1c <5.7% is normal; 5.7–6.4% is pre-diabetes; ≥6.5% is diabetes; transient stress hyperglycaemia resolves with illness. (Book p917)

items.q: An asymptomatic patient has HbA1c 7.2% on one occasion. The next step is:
opts: Repeat the test on a different day to confirm
items.exp: Without symptoms, the test should be repeated; if confirmed, lifestyle and metformin are typical first steps. (Book p917)

items.q: Which value on this page is the diagnostic cut-off for HbA1c?
items.exp: HbA1c ≥6.5% is the diagnostic cut-off; 5.7–6.4% defines pre-diabetes. (Book p917)

items.q: An HbA1c of 5.7–6.4% on this page defines ___.
items.exp: HbA1c 5.7–6.4% indicates increased risk for diabetes (pre-diabetes); 6.5% is the diagnostic cut-off. (Book p917)

items.q: Assess additional tests: I Oral glucose tolerance test is more sensitive than FPG. IIGAD antibody screening is part of routine diagnosis.
items.exp: OGTT is more sensitive than FPG for detecting IGT; GAD antibodies are used for classification after diagnosis, not routine diagnosis. (Book p917)
